html:
The Bantu peoples are the several hundred ethnic groups who speak Bantu languages, spread across Central, East and Southern Africa. The map uses the name for the farming peoples of the Congo basin and its edges from 800 to 1500, before the rise of the large kingdoms there.

They were the heirs of the long Bantu expansion, which had carried farming, iron working and related languages from the borders of Nigeria and Cameroon across half the continent over the previous two thousand years.

How most people lived in these centuries:

  • farming yams, sorghum and millet, and in the wetter forest bananas and plantains, which had come from Asia;
  • fishing in the great rivers and lakes, and keeping goats and, where tsetse flies allowed, cattle;
  • smelting iron and copper, which was traded and made into crosses and bars used as money;
  • living in villages under chiefs, often linked by ties of kinship and marriage.

Over time some chiefdoms grew into states. In the Upemba depression of Katanga, rich graves show growing wealth from the 700s, the background to the later Luba kingdom. In the west the Kingdom of Kongo formed around 1400. Further east and south, Bantu speakers founded the towns of the Swahili coast and built Great Zimbabwe. After 1500 the Lunda and others turned these networks into empires. Today about one in three Africans speaks a Bantu language.
